Question three. How do you choose a chunking strategy? It's precision against context. Small chunks match precisely, but can lose the context the answer needs. Large chunks keep context, but one vector must cover several topics, so retrieval gets fuzzier, and each hit takes more of the context window. Common choices: a fixed size, say three to five hundred tokens, overlapping ten to twenty percent, so a sentence cut at a boundary is whole in one chunk. Structure-aware: split on headings and paragraphs, then merge toward the target. Or small-to-big: retrieve small chunks, send the parent section. No universal best: measure retrieval recall on labeled real questions, and store the chunk settings with the index version, since changing them means a rebuild.

Question four. How do you keep embeddings fresh without re-embedding everything? Treat it as an incremental load: give every chunk a stable id and a content hash, and compare with what's indexed. In the page's example, doc one, chunk one changed, and doc three is new: embed those two. Doc two is gone: delete it. Doc one, chunk zero costs nothing. Skip the deletes, and a removed document keeps answering questions. Wrong at best, a data leak at worst.

Question five. What changes when you switch embedding models? Everything gets re-embedded. Each model has its own space, so a new model's query can't be compared with old documents. Here's a tiny space of five words. Pretend a second model learned the same meanings with its axes in another order. Its kitten, searched in the old index, lands nearest truck. So treat it like a blue-green deployment: build a new index version beside the old, backfill and compare, then switch an alias atomically, and keep the old one for rollback. And store the model version on every vector, so a mixed index can't happen silently.
